chapters.title: Chapter 3: Unconstrained Optimization: Gradients, Hessians, and Critical Points

lessons.title: The Gradient: Direction of Steepest Ascent

children.text: Chapter 2 proved that the answer Ananya is looking for is guaranteed to exist and be unique. It did not show her how to find it. The next interview round is computational: given a covariance matrix and a starting set of weights, calculate the actual direction that reduces risk fastest. That direction has a name, the gradient, and it is the single most-used tool for the rest of this course.

body.text: The gradient is a vector that points in the direction a function increases fastest. It is the natural generalization of slope to functions of many variables, and every method in this course, from plain calculus to Lagrange multipliers to KKT conditions, is built on top of it.

markDefs.definition: The derivative of a multi-variable function with respect to one variable, treating every other variable as a fixed constant. Written with a curly d symbol, like df/dw1.

children.text: For a single-variable function, f'(x) tells you the slope, how fast f changes as x moves. A portfolio has many weights at once, so a single number cannot capture how variance changes as you nudge each weight separately. The fix is a
for each variable, one at a time, stacked into a single vector called the gradient.

body.latex: \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}, \ldots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \right)
body.caption: The gradient: one partial derivative per variable, collected into a vector of the same length as x.

children.text: Partial Derivatives: Holding Everything Else Fixed
Return to the toy objective from Chapter 1, f(x1, x2) = x1² + x2². To find the partial derivative with respect to x1, treat x2 as if it were a fixed number, like 7, and differentiate normally.

body.latex: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} = 2x_1, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} = 2x_2 \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \nabla f(x_1, x_2) = (2x_1, \; 2x_2)
body.caption: Each partial derivative only reacts to its own variable. x2² has zero derivative with respect to x1, since it is treated as constant there.

children.text: The Gradient of Portfolio Variance, Computed Numerically

Chapter 2 already derived the gradient of portfolio variance symbolically: 2Σw. Plug in the Reliance-TCS covariance matrix from earlier in the course, and evaluate it at an equal-weighted starting point, w = (0.5, 0.5).

body.caption: Multiply the covariance matrix by the weight vector first.
Double it. This is the gradient of portfolio variance at the 50/50 Reliance-TCS portfolio.

body.text: Read the two entries against each other. The gradient's first entry, 0.0952, is larger than its second, 0.0744. That means variance is more sensitive to changes in w1 (Reliance) than w2 (TCS) at this exact point, which makes sense: Reliance has the higher individual variance of the two (0.0784 vs 0.0576). If you wanted to cut portfolio risk fastest from this starting point, the gradient just told you where to look first: trim Reliance before TCS.

children.text: Among every possible direction you could move from a given point, the gradient vector points in the one direction where the function increases fastest, and its length tells you exactly how fast. Reverse its sign, and you get the direction where the function decreases fastest, called steepest descent. This is not a metaphor, it is a provable fact from calculus: no other direction, of the same step size, increases f by more than moving along the gradient does.

body.label: Negative gradient, -∇f(x)
body.value: Points in the direction of steepest descent
body.context: This single fact is the entire engine behind gradient descent, one of the most widely used optimization algorithms in quant finance and machine learning alike.

children.text: Gradient Equals Zero at a Flat Point

If the gradient points toward the steepest way up, then at the very top or bottom of a smooth, unconstrained function, there is no uphill or downhill direction left. The gradient there must be exactly the zero vector, every entry zero at once.

body.caption: A necessary condition for x* to be an unconstrained minimum (or maximum). The next lesson turns this single equation into the actual method for finding x*.

body.title: Read the gradient
body.question: At a certain point, the gradient of a portfolio's variance with respect to its three weights is (0.12, -0.03, 0.08). In which direction does portfolio variance increase fastest from this point?
options: Increasing w1 and w3 while decreasing w2, in proportion to these values
Decreasing w1 and w3 while increasing w2
Equally in all three weights, since gradients only give magnitude
Impossible to say without knowing the covariance matrix
body.explanation: The gradient vector itself is the direction of steepest ascent. A positive entry means increasing that weight increases the objective; a negative entry means increasing that weight actually decreases it. Here w1 and w3 have positive entries and w2 has a negative one, so moving exactly along (0.12, -0.03, 0.08), increasing w1 and w3 while decreasing w2, increases variance faster than moving in any other direction of the same size.

body.title: Use the gradient to cut risk
body.scenario: You manage a 3-stock portfolio and compute the gradient of portfolio variance at your current weights: (0.02, 0.15, 0.01). The portfolio's risk is higher than you would like.
body.prompt: Based on this gradient, which stock's weight would you reduce first to cut portfolio risk fastest, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Reduce the weight on the second stock first. The gradient's second entry, 0.15, is far larger than the other two, meaning variance is most sensitive to that weight at this point: increasing it raises risk fastest, and by the same logic, decreasing it lowers risk fastest. The steepest-descent direction, roughly the negative of (0.02, 0.15, 0.01) scaled down, is dominated by cutting the second stock's weight, with only minor adjustments to the other two.

cards.definition: The derivative of a multi-variable function with respect to one variable, holding every other variable fixed.
The vector of all partial derivatives of a function, one per variable. Points in the direction of steepest ascent.
The direction, among all possible directions from a point, in which a function increases fastest. Given exactly by the gradient.
The direction in which a function decreases fastest. Given exactly by the negative of the gradient.
A point where every partial derivative is zero at once. A necessary condition for an unconstrained minimum or maximum.

points: The gradient generalizes slope to many variables: a vector holding one partial derivative per variable.
A partial derivative treats every variable except one as a fixed constant, then differentiates normally.
For portfolio variance, the gradient is 2Σw, computable directly by matrix multiplication once you have the covariance matrix and a weight vector.
The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent; its negative points in the direction of steepest descent, the basis of gradient descent algorithms.
At an unconstrained minimum or maximum of a smooth function, the gradient must equal the zero vector. The next lesson builds this into the actual solution method.
